Kuiper Belt. The Kuiper Belt is a vast region of icy bodies orbiting the Sun beyond Neptune, stretching roughly thirty to fifty-five astronomical units from the Sun. Composed of dwarf planets, comets, and smaller icy objects, it is the source of short-period comets and home to Pluto, which was reclassified as a dwarf planet in two thousand six. The belt's discovery in the nineteen-nineties fundamentally revised our understanding of the outer solar system's structure and population.

The Kuiper Belt is named after Dutch-American astronomer Gerard Kuiper, who predicted its existence in nineteen fifty-one. It was not directly observed until nineteen ninety-two.

It contains at least one hundred thousand objects larger than one hundred kilometers in diameter, mostly composed of frozen methane, ammonia, and water ice.

Pluto was long considered the ninth planet and was discovered in nineteen thirty by Clyde Tombaugh. Its two thousand six reclassification as a dwarf planet sparked debate because it shares many traits with Kuiper Belt objects.

Other notable dwarf planets in the Kuiper Belt include Eris, Haumea, and Makemake. Eris is actually more massive than Pluto.

The belt is the primary source of short-period comets—those with orbital periods under two hundred years—ejected from their stable orbits by gravitational perturbations.

Objects in the Kuiper Belt orbit in nearly circular, low-inclination paths. This orderly structure contrasts with the spherical, high-inclination Oort Cloud beyond.

The New Horizons spacecraft, launched in two thousand six, performed a historic flyby of Pluto in two thousand fifteen, revealing a geologically diverse, complex world.
